topic: Minimal self-hosted execution path for scoped agent authority on BSC (chain 56) — EIP-7702 self-relay, no bundler, no vendor lock-in
executive_summary: A fully self-hosted path exists on BSC today and it is better than the bundler path. Verified live via BSC RPC (chain 0x38, Geth v1.7.7): the MetaMask Delegation Framework v1.3.0 is deployed on chain 56 — DelegationManager 0xdb9B1e94B5b69Df7e401DDbedE43491141047dB3 (11.5KB code), EIP7702StatelessDeleGatorImpl 0x63c0c19a282a1B52b07dD5a65b58948A07DAE32B (11.2KB), plus every caveat enforcer AiKi needs: ERC20PeriodTransferEnforcer, TimestampEnforcer, AllowedTargetsEnforcer, AllowedMethodsEnforcer, ValueLteEnforcer, LimitedCallsEnforcer, RedeemerEnforcer, MultiTokenPeriodEnforcer. Crucially ERC20PeriodTransferEnforcer is a RESETTING per-period cap ("the transferable amount resets at the beginning of each period"), which fixes the exact gap in Rhinestone's SmartSession on BSC, where ERC20SpendingLimitPolicy is lifetime-only and TimeFrame/UsageLimit/ValueLimit are not deployed at all. eth-infinitism's Simple7702Account is also live at 0xe6Cae83BdE06E4c305530e199D7217f42808555B (3.6KB) but enforces nothing — it is a batching shim, not scoped authority. Recommended path: AiKi self-relays a type-0x4 SetCode tx with viem 2.55.19 (`signAuthorization({account, contractAddress})` → `sendTransaction({authorizationList, to, data})`) to delegate the user EOA to EIP7702StatelessDeleGatorImpl, then AiKi's relayer calls `redeemDelegations` as the delegate and pays all gas in BNB. No bundler, no EntryPoint, no paymaster, no vendor API key. Estimated 5-8 eng days vs 8-14 for the 4337 route and 10-15 plus audit for a bespoke session-key contract. One honest caveat: DelegationManager carries a `whenNotPaused` modifier, so this is not zero third-party dependency — build a thin fallback executor behind an interface.

findings.claim: EIP-7702 self-relay works on BSC with a plain RPC and no bundler; viem 2.55.19 exposes signAuthorization + sendTransaction({authorizationList})
findings.detail: Verified npm registry: viem latest is 2.55.19 (fetched 2026-08-19), confirming the 2.55.x line. viem docs give the exact shape: `walletClient.signAuthorization({ account: eoa, contractAddress })` returns an Authorization with fields `chainId`, `contractAddress`, `nonce`, `r`, `s`, `yParity`. The field is `contractAddress`, NOT `address`. Optional params: `chainId` (defaults to client chain), `nonce` (defaults to the account's next nonce), and `executor: 'self' | undefined`. Set `executor: 'self'` ONLY when the same account that signed the authorization also sends the transaction (this changes the nonce accounting). For AiKi's sponsored model the relayer is a different account, so `executor` is omitted. The transaction is then a normal `eth_sendRawTransaction` of a type-0x4 envelope: `sendTransaction({ authorizationList: [authorization], to: eoa.address, data })`. There is no bundler, no EntryPoint, and no ERC-4337 UserOperation anywhere in this path. BSC accepts type 0x4 since Pascal (2025-03-20, previously verified).

findings.claim: Two 7702 delegation targets are confirmed live on BSC by direct eth_getCode — but only one enforces anything
findings.detail: Queried https://bsc-dataseed.bnbchain.org (eth_chainId = 0x38, clientVersion Geth/v1.7.7) on 2026-08-19. Simple7702Account (eth-infinitism, the EntryPoint v0.8 'delegatee' address per Candide docs): 0xe6Cae83BdE06E4c305530e199D7217f42808555B returns 7316 hex chars (~3.6KB bytecode) — DEPLOYED. MetaMask EIP7702StatelessDeleGatorImpl: 0x63c0c19a282a1B52b07dD5a65b58948A07DAE32B returns 22408 bytes (~11.2KB) — DEPLOYED. EntryPoint v0.8 0x4337084D9E255Ff0702461CF8895CE9E3b5Ff108 returns 43514 bytes, re-confirming prior research. The critical distinction: Simple7702Account gives batching and 4337 compatibility but has NO scoping primitive — an EOA delegated to it grants all-or-nothing authority to itself, so AiKi would have to hold the user's key or enforce limits purely off-chain. EIP7702StatelessDeleGatorImpl stores no signer state (control is granted to the EOA sharing the same address) and is the entry point into the caveat-enforced delegation system. For scoped agent authority, Simple7702Account is the wrong target. Kernel/Safe7702 addresses were not resolved and remain unverified.

findings.claim: MetaMask Delegation Framework v1.3.0 (ERC-7710) is deployed on BSC mainnet — contracts confirmed by bytecode, not just documentation
findings.detail: The framework's Deployments.md lists 'Binance Smart Chain' in its mainnet set and states deployments use a CREATE2 salt of 'GATOR' so addresses are identical across chains. I verified this against chain 56 rather than trusting the doc. eth_getCode on 2026-08-19 returned non-empty bytecode for: DelegationManager 0xdb9B1e94B5b69Df7e401DDbedE43491141047dB3 (23044 bytes), SimpleFactory 0x69Aa2f9fe1572F1B640E1bbc512f5c3a734fc77c (1540), ERC20PeriodTransferEnforcer 0x474e3Ae7E169e940607cC624Da8A15Eb120139aB (6730), TimestampEnforcer 0x1046bb45C8d673d4ea75321280DB34899413c069 (2548), AllowedTargetsEnforcer 0x7F20f61b1f09b08D970938F6fa563634d65c4EeB (3730), AllowedMethodsEnforcer 0x2c21fD0Cb9DC8445CB3fb0DC5E7Bb0Aca01842B5 (4126), ValueLteEnforcer 0x92Bf12322527cAA612fd31a0e810472BBB106A8F (2582), LimitedCallsEnforcer 0x04658B29F6b82ed55274221a06Fc97D318E25416 (2552), RedeemerEnforcer 0xE144b0b2618071B4E56f746313528a669c7E65c5 (3260), ERC20StreamingEnforcer 0x56c97aE02f233B29fa03502Ecc0457266d9be00e (5920), MultiTokenPeriodEnforcer 0xFB2f1a9BD76d3701B730E5d69C3219D42D80eBb7 (10556), NativeTokenPeriodTransferEnforcer 0x9BC0FAf4Aca5AE429F4c06aEEaC517520CB16BD9 (5844). Byte counts are JSON response sizes, all far above an empty '0x' result.

findings.claim: ERC20PeriodTransferEnforcer is a RESETTING periodic cap — this is the single most important finding, because it closes the gap Rhinestone leaves open on BSC
findings.detail: Read from source. Natspec: 'The transferable amount resets at the beginning of each period, and any unused tokens are forfeited once the period ends.' Confirmed in `_getAvailableAmount`: `uint256 alreadyTransferred = isNewPeriod_ ? 0 : _allowance.transferredInCurrentPeriod;`. Terms are a packed 116-byte blob: token address (bytes 0-19), periodAmount uint256 (20-51), periodDuration in seconds (52-83), startDate timestamp (84-115). It requires the call's calldata selector to equal `IERC20.transfer.selector` (0xa9059cbb) and emits `TransferredInPeriod`. Errors include 'transfer-amount-exceeded', 'transfer-not-started', 'invalid-zero-period-amount', 'invalid-zero-period-duration', 'invalid-zero-start-date'. Contrast with prior verified research: Rhinestone's ERC20SpendingLimitPolicy on BSC is a LIFETIME cap with monotonic alreadySpent and no block.timestamp, and the TimeFrame/UsageLimit/ValueLimit policies are NOT deployed on 56. So 'agent may spend 50 BUSD per day' is expressible on BSC via the MetaMask framework and is NOT expressible via Rhinestone SmartSession on BSC. Note the selector restriction: this enforcer covers transfer only, not approve or transferFrom.

findings.claim: What the chain enforces in the ERC-7710 path: signature, authority chain, delegate identity, revocation, and every caveat hook
findings.detail: From DelegationManager.sol source. Entry point is `redeemDelegations(bytes[] _permissionContexts, ModeCode[] _modes, bytes[] _executionCallDatas) external whenNotPaused`. On-chain validation, all unavoidable by AiKi: (1) delegator signature — ECDSA.recover must equal delegation.delegator, else InvalidEOASignature; for contract delegators IERC1271.isValidSignature must return the magic value; (2) authority chain linkage — each delegation's `authority` must equal the next delegation hash, and the terminal one must equal ROOT_AUTHORITY; (3) delegate chain — successive delegates must match delegators unless ANY_DELEGATE; (4) caller identity — `if (delegations_[0].delegate != msg.sender && delegations_[0].delegate != ANY_DELEGATE) revert InvalidDelegate()`; (5) revocation — `if (disabledDelegations[hash]) revert CannotUseADisabledDelegation()`; (6) caveat hooks — beforeAllHook and beforeHook on every enforcer before execution, afterHook and afterAllHook in reverse order after. Structs: Delegation{delegator, delegate, authority, caveats[], salt, signature}, Caveat{enforcer, terms, args}. Everything else — which agent may act, task semantics, marketplace policy, UX — is enforced by AiKi off-chain and is not a chain guarantee.

findings.claim: Gas sponsorship is trivially solved by self-relay: AiKi's relayer is the tx sender and pays BNB; the user never holds BNB and never signs a transaction
findings.detail: There are two separate sponsored moments. (a) Delegation install: the user signs only an EIP-7702 authorization tuple off-chain (chainId, contractAddress, nonce, r, s, yParity). AiKi wraps it in `authorizationList` of a transaction AiKi sends and pays for. Because the executor is AiKi and not the signer, do NOT pass `executor: 'self'`. (b) Action execution: AiKi's relayer EOA is the `delegate` and calls DelegationManager.redeemDelegations directly, satisfying the `delegations_[0].delegate == msg.sender` check, and pays gas. No paymaster, no EntryPoint, no bundler, no deposit staking. Trust implications, stated honestly: AiKi gains liveness power (ordering, timing, censorship, refusal to relay) but NOT custody — it cannot exceed the caveats, because the enforcers revert. Real risks to design around: 7702 authorization signed with chainId 0 is replayable on every chain, so always pin chainId 56; the authorization nonce is the user EOA's account nonce, so any user-initiated transaction in between invalidates a pre-signed authorization and requires re-signing; a compromised relayer key can act freely within caveat bounds, so scope one delegate key per agent and keep periods tight.

findings.claim: Honest three-way comparison for a 3-week deadline: 7702 self-relay + delegation framework wins on both risk and eng days
findings.detail: Option A, bundler ERC-4337: EntryPoint v0.6/v0.7/v0.8 are live on 56, but this route reintroduces the exact vendor dependency being avoided (bundler RPC, paymaster service, API keys, rate limits), and on BSC the Rhinestone policy set cannot express a resetting daily cap. Est. 8-14 eng days including vendor evaluation, UserOperation plumbing, paymaster integration, module install flows, plus unquantified vendor-availability risk. Option B, 7702 self-relay + MetaMask Delegation Framework: plain RPC, contracts already deployed and verified on 56, richest on-chain policy set available on this chain. Est. 5-8 eng days: 1-2 for the 7702 authorization and relay path, 2-3 for delegation construction/caveat encoding/signing UX, 1 for the relayer service and nonce management, 1-2 for testnet-to-mainnet hardening. Option C, bespoke AiKi session-key contract: maximum control and zero third-party pause risk, but 10-15 eng days plus a 2-4 week audit that does not fit before 9 Sep 2026. Shipping it unaudited while it holds delegated spend authority is the worst risk on the table. Recommendation: B now, C later behind an interface.

findings.claim: The one genuine dependency in Option B: DelegationManager is pausable, so 'no vendor dependency' is not literally true
findings.detail: redeemDelegations carries the `whenNotPaused` modifier. If the DelegationManager owner on BSC pauses the contract, every AiKi delegation redemption halts until unpaused. This is a liveness dependency on a third party — weaker than a bundler dependency (no API key, no rate limit, no per-request business relationship, and the code is immutable and CREATE2-deterministic) but it is not zero. Funds are never at risk from a pause; only the ability to execute is. Two mitigations worth the eng time: (1) put redemption behind an `IAgentExecutor` interface in AiKi's relayer so a fallback path can be swapped in without touching call sites; (2) build the minimal bespoke session-key executor from Option C as a post-deadline fallback, since it becomes cheap once the delegation-encoding and relayer layers already exist. I did not verify the pause owner's identity or whether it is a multisig/timelock on chain 56 — that check should happen before mainnet launch, since it determines how real this risk is.

interfaces.source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MetaMask/delegation-framework/main/documents/Deployments.md, each address confirmed non-empty by eth_getCode on chain 56

gaps: Did NOT verify that the @metamask/delegation-toolkit npm package supports chain 56 in its own chain config. The CONTRACTS are on BSC (bytecode-confirmed), but the SDK may not ship a 56 entry — budget half a day to override addresses manually, and treat the SDK as optional since redeemDelegations can be called with a raw viem ABI.

ERC-7715 (wallet_grantPermissions) support in the MetaMask wallet client for BSC is entirely unverified. ERC-7710 on-chain redemption is confirmed; the wallet-side permission-request UX is not. Do not assume users can grant via MetaMask UI on BSC — AiKi likely needs its own signing flow for the Delegation struct (EIP-712).

Never sent a live type-0x4 transaction. eth_getCode reads confirm deployment; they do not prove that public BSC RPC providers accept eth_sendRawTransaction for type 0x4 envelopes. Send one throwaway 7702 tx on BSC testnet then mainnet in week 1 — this is the single highest-value de-risking action and costs under an hour.

DelegationManager's pause authority on chain 56 was not inspected — owner address, whether it is an EOA/multisig/timelock. This determines whether the whenNotPaused dependency is a footnote or a real risk. Check owner() before mainnet.

Enforcer bytecode was confirmed present but NOT diffed against the audited source, and BscScan source-verification status was not checked. CREATE2 determinism makes a mismatch unlikely but it is unproven.

Kernel (ZeroDev) and Safe7702 implementation addresses on BSC were not resolved — the searches did not surface published 56 addresses. If MetaMask's framework is rejected, these are unmapped alternatives.

EntryPoint v0.9 and Simple7702AccountV09 now exist (Candide docs call V09 'recommended for new integrations'), but neither was verified on chain 56. Irrelevant to the recommended path, which touches no EntryPoint at all.
Gas cost of a type-0x4 SetCode tx and of redeemDelegations on BSC was not measured. Needed to price AiKi's sponsorship burn per user and per agent action.
aiki_implications: Take the 7702 self-relay path and drop the bundler question entirely. The recommended stack is: viem 2.55.19 + a type-0x4 SetCode tx delegating the user EOA to EIP7702StatelessDeleGatorImpl 0x63c0c19a282a1B52b07dD5a65b58948A07DAE32B, then AiKi's relayer calling DelegationManager 0xdb9B1e94B5b69Df7e401DDbedE43491141047dB3. No bundler, no EntryPoint, no paymaster, no API key, no vendor rate limit. Est. 5-8 eng days, which fits the 9 Sep 2026 deadline with margin.

This reverses the earlier Rhinestone-leaning conclusion and should be escalated. Rhinestone SmartSession on BSC cannot express 'agent may spend 50 BUSD per day' — its ERC20SpendingLimitPolicy is a lifetime cap, and TimeFrame/UsageLimit/ValueLimit are not deployed on 56. The MetaMask framework's ERC20PeriodTransferEnforcer resets every period, and TimestampEnforcer/LimitedCallsEnforcer/ValueLteEnforcer are all confirmed live on 56. For a marketplace whose core promise is a recurring bounded budget per agent, this is the difference between shipping the real product and shipping a degraded one.

Be precise in all user-facing and investor-facing copy about the chain/AiKi enforcement split. CHAIN-ENFORCED: per-period spend ceiling, delegation expiry, target-contract allowlist, method-selector allowlist, native-value ceiling, call count, which agent key may redeem, delegator signature validity, revocation via disabledDelegations. AIKI-ENFORCED (trust us, off-chain): agent selection and reputation, task semantics, pricing, matching, whether a spend was 'appropriate', and relay liveness/ordering. Never let marketing blur the second list into the first.

Design the delegation as one delegation per agent per user, with a distinct delegate key per agent. RedeemerEnforcer pins redemption to a specific key, so a compromise of one agent's relayer key cannot touch another agent's authority. Combine with a short TimestampEnforcer window so stale delegations expire without requiring an on-chain revoke.

Block approve() explicitly. ERC20PeriodTransferEnforcer only constrains calldata whose selector is IERC20.transfer (0xa9059cbb) — it says nothing about approve or transferFrom. Without AllowedMethodsEnforcer (0x2c21fD0Cb9DC8445CB3fb0DC5E7Bb0Aca01842B5) restricting selectors, an agent could grant an unlimited allowance to a third party and drain around the period cap. This is the most likely way to ship a fake safety guarantee.

Handle the 7702 nonce coupling in the relayer from day one. The authorization's nonce is the user EOA's account nonce, so any user-initiated transaction between signing and relaying silently invalidates it. Detect this, re-request the signature, and never leave a user staring at an unexplained failure — this will otherwise be the top support issue at launch.

Pin chainId 56 in every signAuthorization call. chainId 0 authorizations are valid on every EVM chain; signing one would let the same user signature install a delegation on chains AiKi never intended. Make this a lint rule, not a convention.

Budget one day in week 1 to send a real type-0x4 transaction on BSC testnet and mainnet. Everything in this research is read-only verification; the entire plan rests on public BSC RPCs accepting type-0x4 envelopes, which is assumed from Pascal but untested here.

Put redemption behind an IAgentExecutor interface. DelegationManager's whenNotPaused modifier is a genuine third-party liveness dependency — smaller than a bundler dependency, but real. The abstraction costs about half a day now and makes the bespoke session-key executor a drop-in later, converting Option C from a rewrite into a post-deadline upgrade.

Note that AiKi's sponsorship model becomes very clean: users need zero BNB and never sign a transaction, only an off-chain authorization and an EIP-712 delegation. That is a materially better onboarding story than the 4337 route and worth featuring — but price it first, since AiKi pays gas for both the delegation install and every agent action.
